title: The Arrival Trap
author: Mike Fisher
summary: Mike Fisher starts from the viral claim that Forbes 30 Under 30 honorees raised $5.3 billion and committed $18.5 billion in fraud, shows the comparison is misleading, and then asks what kind of environment makes faking success at 25 feel rational. He names the answer the arrival trap: the belief that success has a deadline and that arriving late is the same as never arriving. He cites Census-based research finding the average founder is 42 and the best-performing startups have founders around 45, so the youth premium is a story rather than data. The Charlie Javice case shows what happens when a real but modest business is stretched to meet the culture's clock, and Goodhart's Law explains why age at arrival becomes a bad target. For leaders, he argues that organisations have their own 30 Under 30 and should reward learning velocity over announcement velocity and tell success stories with their real, slow timelines.
points: The viral 30 Under 30 fraud statistic compares mismatched numbers, and the real lesson is about the pressure to look successful early.
Research on millions of U.S. founders shows the average founder is 42 and older founders are more likely to build top-performing companies.
When age at arrival becomes a target, it distorts behaviour from outright fraud to inflated metrics, job-hopping and premature transformation announcements.
Leaders shape the trap by whom they celebrate, so rewarding learning velocity over announcement velocity changes what people optimise.
Telling the real timeline of success, including the boring middle years, stops teams from inheriting an impossible clock.
quotes: A better question is, what kind of environment makes faking success at 25 feel like a rational move?
It runs on the belief that success has a deadline, and that arriving late counts the same as never arriving. Let’s call it the arrival trap.

Using U.S. Census records covering about 2.7 million founders whose companies employed at least one person between 2007 and 2014, they found the average founder was 42 at the time of founding. Among the top 0.1% of startups by growth, the average was 45.
Their records show it comes from reps. We started the clock when the cameras showed up.
This is Goodhart’s Law wearing a hoodie or a Patagonia vest. When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure, and we have made “age at arrival” a target.
When you hand recognition to the fastest arrivals, everyone downstream adjusts. People stop asking “what should I learn here?” and start asking “how does this look?

Reward learning velocity over announcement velocity. When you tell success stories inside your company, tell the real timeline, boring middle years included, because each time a leader compresses an origin story, the team inherits an impossible clock.
